Jerlov water types · 0–100 m

The colour of daylight on the way down

Ten columns of sea water, from the clearest open ocean (I) to the most turbid coastal water (9C). Each band shows the colour of the sunlight that is left at that depth, with the sunlight at the surface taken as white. Pick a column and a depth to read the numbers.

Ten materials, lit from above at this depth

Left half: under the surface sunlight. Right half: at the chosen depth, with the exposure raised until the white PVC is as bright as at the surface and the white balance left at the surface. The object is right in front of the viewer, so no water lies between them. Measured reflectances from the USGS Spectral Library 7.

What this page assumes

  • Kd is the surface type's all the way down. Real water changes with depth; jerlov's descend follows the typical profile of Williamson & Hollins (2023), which moves the PAR 1 % depth of type I from {{I_ONE_KD}} m to {{I_LAYERED}} m. It is not used here.
  • Jerlov's Kd belongs to one sun. His tables do not say which; the surface spectrum here is for a sun {{SUN}}° from the zenith, and Kd is not changed for it.
  • Only 380–700 nm count, the range where both the sky model and Kd are given here. The surface spectrum over the same range is the white.
  • Colours are what a camera white-balanced at the surface would record, not a prediction of what an eye adapted to the water sees. Many of them lie outside sRGB and are clipped.
  • No light scattered towards the viewer from the water in between (no haze), no reflection from the sea floor, no shade. The materials are lit only by downwelling light.
  • This shows light, not visibility. How far an object can be seen is a different question that this page does not answer.

Where the numbers come from

  • Kd: N. G. Jerlov, Marine Optics (Elsevier, 1976), Table XXVII, printed at 16 wavelengths from 310 to 700 nm and read at 1 nm from the dataset that interpolates it.
  • Sunlight just below the surface: Gregg & Carder (1990), Limnol. Oceanogr. 35, 1657–1675, doi:10.4319/lo.1990.35.8.1657, clear sky, sun {{SUN}}° from the zenith, 21 June, visibility {{VISIBILITY}} km, and the standard atmosphere of their Table 5.
  • Colour: CIE 1931 2° observer, sRGB (IEC 61966-2-1).
  • Materials: USGS Spectral Library Version 7 (Kokaly et al. 2017), CC0.
  • All inputs were taken from jerlov , the Python package that collects these sources. The page only multiplies and integrates; its colours and PAR values match jerlov's own spectrum_to_srgb and par_profile to within 0.00001, which a test in its repository checks.
